title: Event-driven architecture is a cultural choice, not a technical one
excerpt: The hardest part of going event-driven is not the infrastructure — it is getting teams to stop thinking in synchronous terms.
body:
I have seen event-driven architecture migrations succeed technically and fail organisationally more often than the reverse. The infrastructure is the easy part. The hard part is getting engineering teams to change how they think about system boundaries, ownership, and failure.

The mental model shift

In a synchronous system, a service call is a transaction: I ask, you answer, we both move on. In an event-driven system, a service publishes a fact about something that happened. It does not know or care who is listening. Consumers react to that fact in their own time, according to their own logic.

This is a fundamentally different relationship between services — and between teams. It requires teams to think about their service as a publisher of a reliable event stream, not as an API endpoint. It requires consumers to think about how they handle delivery failures, reordering, and duplicate events. These are not complicated ideas, but they are different ideas, and changing how people think is slower than changing infrastructure.

Where migrations typically stall

The migrations I have seen stall almost always do so at the same point: when a team needs to coordinate a complex multi-step operation across services and reaches for a synchronous pattern because it feels simpler. It is simpler — right up until the moment it fails in a way that is difficult to recover from. The investment in building event-driven choreography for complex operations pays back compoundingly, but the upfront cost feels real and the future benefit feels abstract.
